newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil credit curbs not necessary for now - Malan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil credit curbs not necessary for now - Malan.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said the government is not considering adopting credit restrictions for the moment.
"When we really find it is necessary to restrict credit, we do so. At the moment we do not consider it necessary," Malan told reporters.
Malan also confirmed earlier remarks by Central Bank chief Gustavo Loyola that there are no plans to weigh restrictive measures at the next meeting of the National Monetary Council (CMN) on April 24.
He added that the government is monitoring the economy carefully.

"We follow carefully all economic indicators and we reserve the right to take the measures when we judge them necessary," he said at the swearing-in ceremony of the new president of the Brazilian Association of International Banks.
Malan's and Loyola's comments came amid mounting market speculation of an imminent move to restrict consumption in an attempt to slow the deterioration of Brazil's external accounts.
They also follow this week's decision by Brazil's Central Bank to leave monthly interest rates for May unchanged from April's 1.58 percent.
Asked if the decision was taken to curb consumption, Malan said it was more related to a 25 basis point increase in U.S. interest rates late March.
He noted "the Central Bank's attitude was preemptive" as the U.S. Federal Reserve could raise rates further.
In addition, policy-makers held rates steady in anticipation of higher market liquidity next month, which by itself could bring down market interest rates, the Central Bank's Loyola said.
